title: Greedy Best-First Rushes to Auckland’s Fastest Route
description: Watch Greedy Best-First sprint across real street-map nodes in Ponsonby, always expanding the “closest-looking” frontier. It’s fast, visually intuitive, and teaches how heuristics guide graph search behavior.
ig_caption:
🚦 Ponsonby streets in Auckland—now let’s watch **Greedy Best-First** make decisions in real time! 🌿

Here’s what the algorithm is doing under the hood: on each step, it picks the next node with the **lowest heuristic value** (typically estimated distance-to-goal). ⚙️ That means it follows *what looks promising* rather than guaranteeing the globally shortest path like Dijkstra/A*. In graph terms, we run a best-first search on a street-map graph where intersections are nodes and road segments are edges. 🗺️

When the heuristic is accurate, it feels incredibly sharp and “smart” — but if the heuristic misleads (e.g., detours or tricky road geometry), the route may be quick without being optimal. 📉✨

👇 Want me to visualize how changing the heuristic impacts the path quality? Drop a comment with your preferred goal (e.g., “from café to coast”) and hit follow for more coding-on-real-maps reels! 💻❤️
fb_caption:
Auckland (Ponsonby) just turned into a graph search playground! 🌆 In this visualization, **Greedy Best-First** expands the next street node that *appears* closest to the destination using a heuristic—fast, intuitive, and perfect for learning how graph search works on real maps. 🗺️

Like, share, and comment what you want to see next: should we compare it against Dijkstra or A* on the same route? 🤓
yt_description:
Greedy Best-First Pathfinding in Auckland (Ponsonby)! 🌿
In this YouTube Shorts video, we visualize how **Greedy Best-First search** works on a real-world street-map graph—intersections as nodes, roads as edges, and a heuristic guiding the frontier.

✅ Keywords: greedy best first, pathfinding visualization, graph search algorithm, heuristic search, real map algorithms, computerscience

Mechanics: the algorithm repeatedly selects the open node with the smallest estimated distance to the goal, which makes it quick but not always shortest.

Watch till the end and comment: should I run A* next to compare optimality vs speed? 🚀
